title: Cluster Upgrades with kubeadm
intro: Upgrading a kubeadm cluster is a specific, ordered procedure — control plane first, one minor version at a time, then each worker node. Skipping steps or versions is how clusters break.

steps.prompt: Check what kubeadm thinks the current and available versions are before touching anything.
steps.fake_output:
[upgrade/versions] Cluster version: v1.29.4
[upgrade/versions] kubeadm version: v1.30.1
Upgrade to the latest version in the v1.30 series:
COMPONENT                 CURRENT   TARGET
kube-apiserver             v1.29.4   v1.30.1
kube-controller-manager    v1.29.4   v1.30.1
kube-scheduler             v1.29.4   v1.30.1
steps.explanation: This is a dry-run — it tells you exactly what would change without touching anything, which is why it's always the first step.
steps.why: Kubernetes only officially supports upgrading one minor version at a time (1.29 to 1.30, not 1.29 to 1.31 directly) — 'upgrade plan' is what confirms you're not about to attempt an unsupported jump.

steps.prompt: Apply the upgrade to the control plane node.
steps.fake_output: [upgrade/successful] SUCCESS! Your cluster was upgraded to "v1.30.1". Enjoy!
steps.explanation: This upgrades the control plane components (kube-apiserver, controller-manager, scheduler, etcd if needed) on this node — kubelet itself is upgraded separately via the OS package manager, not by kubeadm.
steps.why: 'kubeadm upgrade apply' is only run once, on the FIRST control plane node — additional control plane nodes use 'kubeadm upgrade node' instead, since they just need to join the already-upgraded configuration.

steps.prompt: Before upgrading a worker node's kubelet, drain it so its pods reschedule elsewhere safely.
steps.fake_output:
node/node-2 cordoned
evicting pod default/web-abc
node/node-2 drained
steps.explanation: Same drain command from earlier tutorials — upgrading a node's kubelet means it'll restart, so anything still scheduled there would get disrupted mid-upgrade without this step.
steps.why: This is why cordon/drain matter for more than just manual maintenance — every real kubeadm upgrade procedure includes exactly this step for every single worker node, one at a time, never all at once.

steps.prompt: After upgrading kubelet and kubeadm on that node's OS packages, tell kubeadm to update that node's local config to match the new control plane.
steps.fake_output:
[upgrade] The configuration for this node was successfully updated!
[upgrade] Now you should go ahead and upgrade the kubelet package
steps.explanation: This is the worker-node equivalent of 'kubeadm upgrade apply' — it updates the local kubelet configuration to match what the upgraded control plane expects.
steps.why: Every node except the very first control plane node uses 'kubeadm upgrade node', not 'apply' — 'apply' is specifically the one-time command that upgrades the cluster's actual configuration; every other node just needs to catch up to it.

steps.prompt: Bring node-2 back into rotation now that its upgrade is complete.
steps.explanation: Same as any other maintenance drain — uncordon re-enables scheduling, completing the per-node upgrade cycle.
steps.why: This is the last step of the per-node loop in a real upgrade: cordon/drain, upgrade kubelet+kubeadm, kubeadm upgrade node, uncordon — repeated for every worker node, one at a time, never in parallel.
